prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

Ay, gaze upon her rose-wreathed hair, And gaze upon her smile; Seem as you drank the very air Her breath perfumed the while: And wake for her the gifted line, That wild and witching lay, And swear your heart is as a shrine, That only owns her sway. ’Tis well: I am revenged at last,— Mark you that scornful cheek,— The eye averted as you pass’d, Spoke more than words could speak. Ay, now by all the bitter tears That I have shed for thee,— The racking doubts, the burning fears,— Avenged they well may be— By the nights pass’d in sleepless care, The days of endless woe; All that you taught my heart to bear, All that yourself will know. I would not wish to see you laid Within an early tomb; I should forget how you betray’d, And only weep your doom: But this is fitting punishment, To live and love in vain,— Oh my wrung heart, be thou content, And feed upon his pain. Go thou and watch her lightest sigh,— Thine own it will not be; And bask beneath her sunny eye,— It will not turn on thee. ’Tis well: the rack, the chain, the wheel, Far better hadst thou proved; Ev’n I could almost pity feel, For thou art not beloved.

Keywords: And, Seem, Her

outputs.L1:
Ay, gaze upon her rose-wreathed hair,  
And gaze upon her smile;  
Seem as though you drank the very air  
Her breath perfumed the while.  
And wake for her the gifted line,  
That wild and witching lay;  
And swear your heart is as a shrine  
That owns her sway alone.

’Tis well: I am revenged at last—  
Mark well that scornful cheek;  
The eye averted as you passed  
Spoke more than words could speak.  
Ay, now, by all the bitter tears  
That I have shed for thee—  
The racking doubts, the burning fears—  
Well avenged they may be;

By nights passed in sleepless care,  
By days of endless woe;  
By all you taught my heart to bear,  
And all that you shall know.  
I would not wish to see you laid  
Within an early tomb;  
I should forget how you betrayed  
And only weep your doom.

But this is fitting punishment:  
To live and love in vain.  
Oh, my wrung heart, be thou content,  
And feed upon his pain.  
Go thou and watch her lightest sigh—  
Thine own it will not be;  
And bask beneath her sunny eye—  
It will not turn on thee.

’Tis well: the rack, the chain, the wheel  
Far better hadst thou proved.  
Even I could almost pity feel,  
For thou art not beloved.
outputs.L2:
Look at the roses woven through her hair;  
Lose yourself in the brightness of her smile.  
Breathe as though the surrounding air  
Had been sweetened by her breath.  
Compose for her your finest verses,  
A haunting song alive with enchantment,  
And declare that your heart is sacred ground  
Where she alone commands devotion.

Good—my revenge has finally come.  
Did you notice the contempt upon her face?  
When you went by, she turned her eyes away,  
And that gesture said more than speech ever could.

By every bitter tear I cried for you,  
By each tormenting suspicion and fevered fear,  
I say that they have now been fully answered.  
For all my sleepless, anxious nights,  
For all my sorrow-laden days,  
For everything you made my heart endure—  
You yourself will suffer the same.

I would never ask that you die young  
And be placed too soon in the grave;  
Death would make me forget your betrayal,  
Leaving me only to mourn your fate.  
No—this punishment suits you better:  
You must remain alive and love without hope.  
My wounded heart, take comfort now  
And nourish yourself upon his misery.

Go, attend to her faintest breath,  
Knowing that no sigh of hers is meant for you.  
Stand gladly in the warmth of her radiant gaze,  
Though her eyes will never turn your way.  
Yes, this is just: the rack, the chain,  
And even the breaking wheel would have been kinder.  
I can almost find it in me to pity you,  
Because the woman you adore does not love you.
outputs.L3:
The speaker watches as her former lover admires and praises another woman, only to have his affection go unreturned. She sees this rejection as a form of poetic justice, since it mirrors the scorn, betrayal, and emotional suffering he once caused her. His cruelty left her weeping bitterly, enduring sleepless nights, struggling with relentless doubts, and carrying her sorrow for a long time.

Rather than wishing for his death, the speaker believes that living with the torment of unrequited love is a more fitting punishment. To desire someone who remains indifferent allows him to experience the same helplessness and pain that she once endured because of him. Although she briefly feels pity when she sees his suffering, that sympathy quickly fades. In the end, she takes satisfaction in knowing that he now understands what it means to love without being loved in return.
outputs.L4:
The speaker reflects bitterly on a former lover who betrayed her and now devotes himself to another woman. Rather than grieving openly over his rejection, she watches his new courtship with anger and grim satisfaction. Although he longs for the other woman and pursues her with apparent sincerity, his affection remains unreturned. His frustration mirrors the pain he once caused the speaker, turning his romantic failure into a form of poetic justice.

She therefore interprets his suffering as the fitting consequence of his disloyalty. The man who treated her love carelessly must now experience what it means to desire someone who will not return his feelings. His rejection restores a sense of moral balance: he has become vulnerable to the same loneliness, uncertainty, and humiliation that his betrayal inflicted on her.

The speaker’s revenge is primarily emotional rather than physical. She does not wish merely to wound or kill him, since bodily pain would be temporary and death might even release him from suffering. Instead, she wants him to remain alive and conscious of his failure, trapped in an unfulfilled passion that continually torments him. In her view, longing without hope is a punishment more severe than physical violence because it must be endured repeatedly.

Beneath the speaker’s triumph, however, lies evidence of unresolved hurt. Her intense interest in her former lover’s unhappiness suggests that his betrayal still has power over her. By imagining his rejection as revenge, she transforms her own pain into a judgment against him. The poem thus presents love as both desire and punishment, showing how betrayal can turn affection into resentment and how emotional suffering may become the cruelest form of retribution.

It would seem that even after the darkest hours, courage had been waiting patiently inside her.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a Gothic Romantic poem in which a betrayed woman takes bitter satisfaction in seeing her former lover’s new love reject him.
counterfactuals.output:
### **The Second Forsaking**

Beneath the moon’s funereal flame,  
I watched beside the yew,  
When through the ruined abbey’s gate  
Your haggard figure drew.  

Once, in that cloistered dark, you swore  
No dawn could make us part—  
Then laid your vows, like withered wreaths,  
Upon another’s heart.  

She came in silk as pale as mist,  
With winter in her eyes;  
You knelt where once I knelt to you  
And offered gilded lies.  

But she had heard the hollow ring  
Beneath each honeyed word;  
She turned before your pleading ceased,  
As cold as any sword.  

“Keep, sir,” she said, “your faithless love,  
Your kisses bought with pain.  
No woman warms a serpent twice,  
Nor trusts a broken chain.”  

Then down the aisle her footfalls died;  
The chapel doors were thrown,  
And all the ancient, eyeless saints  
Beheld you stand alone.  

You called her name. The rafters wept.  
The bats wheeled black above.  
How strange—your voice had never mourned  
The grave of *my* dead love.  

I should have pitied what remained:  
That face the darkness marred,  
Those hands that clutched at emptiness,  
That proud mouth stricken hard.  

Instead, I pressed my lips to smile  
And tasted blood and rain;  
For every tear I shed for you  
Returned to you as pain.  

Yet triumph is a bitter wine—  
I drank, and still I knew:  
Her scorn could never mend the heart  
That first was slain by you.  

So take the night, the dust, the stones,  
The vows no soul believes.  
I leave you with the only bride  
A faithless lover grieves—  

The shadow of the woman gone,  
The ghost you could not move;  
And in your breast, forevermore,  
The grave of twice-lost love.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a nineteenth-century-style ballad about unrequited love, jealousy, betrayal, and revenge, beginning with “Ay, gaze upon her rose-wreathed hair.”
counterfactuals.output:
Ay, gaze upon her rose-wreathed hair,  
Her brow as white as foam;  
She smiles beside the altar-stair—  
And I must wander home.  

I loved her when the hawthorn blew,  
Ere pride had touched her breast;  
She swore beneath the churchyard yew  
That I alone was blest.  

But gold may buy a maiden’s vow,  
And rank may turn her head;  
Lord Everard claims her kisses now,  
And all our troth lies dead.  

Last night I saw them in the lane,  
Where once she clung to me;  
He kissed her lips in silver rain—  
She laughed beneath the tree.  

“O false of heart! O fair of face!  
Was love so light a thing?”  
She answered, “Love must yield to place,  
And beggars cannot ring.”  

Then jealousy, that coal-black hound,  
Rose baying in my breast;  
I drew the blade no priest had blessed,  
And swore it should not rest.  

At midnight by the ruined mill  
I met her lord alone;  
The moon lay cold upon the hill,  
The river made its moan.  

We crossed our steel; his scarlet blood  
Ran darkly through the rye;  
I cast his body in the flood  
And watched it wheeling by.  

At dawn her bridal bells began,  
Then ceased with one wild cry;  
They found no bridegroom, horse, nor man—  
But I was standing nigh.  

She knew the stain upon my sleeve,  
She knew my ashen brow:  
“Thou hast avenged thy heart,” she breathed,  
“Who shall avenge me now?”  

I kissed the roses from her hair  
And flung them where he lay;  
Then left her weeping on the stair  
Before the break of day.  

Now chains are cold about my feet,  
The rope hangs o’er my head;  
Yet every night her voice is sweet,  
And every rose blooms red.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a rhyming dramatic monologue spoken by a heartbroken woman who tells her faithless beloved that living unloved is a punishment worse than death.
counterfactuals.output:
Go, faithless love—your vows were writ in sand,  
Then swept away beneath another’s hand.  
You leave me breath, yet steal the breath’s delight;  
A dawn that never warms, a starless night.  

Do not suppose I fear the grave’s release—  
The dead, at least, are folded into peace.  
But I must wake where once your promise shone,  
And bear a beating heart that beats alone.  

Death strikes but once; your absence strikes each day,  
A slow, cold blade that will not turn away.  
The tomb is dark, but darker still the breath  
That lives unloved—my punishment past death.  

So take your kisses, spend them where you will;  
Your treason leaves me living, longing still.  
And know, when all your borrowed passions cease:  
You gave me life—and robbed that life of peace.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.output:
Here is an original poem in a Victorian Gothic style, using your requested closing lines:

### **The Unmourned**

Beneath the yew’s funereal shade,  
Where moonlit vapours stray,  
I saw thee stand, a lonely maid,  
More pale than breaking day.  

No friendly step approached the stone,  
No tear bedewed the ground;  
The restless wind, and wind alone,  
Awoke the silence round.  

Thy pride had chilled each faithful breast,  
Thy scorn had friendship moved;  
Yet, seeing thee thus all unblest,  
By none recalled or loved—  

Though wrongs of thine my heart congeal,  
And long my grief has proved,  
Ev’n I could almost pity feel,  
For thou art not beloved.
